catalog_quote: 2.5 Stress Stress is applied to the first syllable of a phonological word. Stress is not contrastive in Bilua. For a diphthong, stress is realised as prominence on the first element. (2.38) ['toupa] 'lake' (2.39) ['uri] 'good' (2.40) ['siɔtolu] 'eight' (2.41) ['ruᵑge] 'bad' (2.42) ['βairutu] 'today/now' Stress, however, may fall on the second syllable of a phonological word when a phonological word does not coincide with a grammatical word. This is described in the next section. ... [2.6, p. 13] Unlike words, clitics do not bear inherent stress, and this suggests that they do not form a phonological word of their own ... Cliticisation does not affect the stress on the host in Bilua. ... Procliticisation does not affect the stress on the host either, and this results in the stress falling on the second syllable of a phonological word ... [p. 14] Like clitics, Bilua VP particles do not bear inherent stress. That is, a Bilua phonological word may consist of morphemes that bear no inherent stress. Such a phonological word, however, still bears stress on the first syllable of the phonological word, following the stress pattern in Bilua

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (Obata 2003, Pacific Linguistics 540; 711-page scan-only scan from ANU Open Research hdl 1885/146708, no text per pdffonts), the compiler scanned file, and the 2000 ANU thesis text hdl 1885/148145). I independently rendered pp. 34 and 35 of to PNG (page render, 90 dpi, no scanned) and read the page scan directly. p. 34 is book p. 12 ('12 Chapter 2' header) and carries, under the heading '2.5 Stress': 'Stress is applied to the first syllable of a phonological word. Stress is not contrastive in Bilua. For a diphthong, stress is realised as prominence on the first element.' followed by (2.38) ['toupa] 'lake', (2.39) ['uri] 'good', (2.40) ['siɔtolu] 'eight', (2.41) ['ruŋge] 'bad'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the phonological word and is non-contrastive. Clitics and affixes carry no stress of their own; enclitics leave initial stress on the host; a (C)V pronominal proclitic joins the host's phonological word without attracting stress, so stress stays on the host's first syllable (= second syllable of the clitic group). A proclitic or VP particle that forms a phonological word on its own is stressed on its first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described as such; reduplicated forms consist of two phonological words, each stressed on its first syllable (e.g. ['toru'toruru] 'round'); compounds take a single stress on the first syllable of the whole word.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitic + host groups surface with stress on the second syllable of the phonological word (first syllable of the host); diphthongs carry prominence on the first element; footnote in the valency chapter (thesis fn. 63) speculates without evidence that a CVC object proclitic might affect host stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (host plus clitics), explicitly distinguished from the grammatical word; examples are citation forms and textual examples with stress marks. Intonational 'strong stress' on linking adverbials (sainio, soinio) is treated separately under intonation/discourse.
new_statements.identity_note: Obata's grammar describes Bilua (blb, bilu1245) as spoken on Vella Lavella, Western Province, Solomon Islands (fieldwork 1990s); no dialect split is made for the stress statement. The 2000 ANU thesis and the 2003 Pacific Linguistics book carry identical wording for section 2.5.

sources.note: Ch. 2 sec. 2.5 (p. 12): stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word; not contrastive; on a diphthong realised on the first element. Sec. 2.6 (pp. 12-14): clitics and affixes bear no inherent stress; proclitics do not shift stress off the host, so a proclitic+host phonological word is stressed on its second syllable (first of the host); VP particles or proclitics forming their own phonological word take initial stress; reduplicants are separate phonological words each with initial stress; compounds carry one initial stress.

tone.quote: The phonology of the languages other than Savosavu [sic scanned; = Savosavo] has not been studied in depth. For purposes of comparison the orthography of Savosavo has been used for the other three languages, with some supplementary symbols as necessary. ... The symbol c is used for affricate [ts] in Baniata, and the sequence ni in both Baniata and Bilua may prove to be a unit ñ. In Lavukaleve vowel length may prove to be significant but has not been indicated, and in Savosavo no rule of automatic stress placement has been formulated so that stress should be marked but is not.
